text_blocks.snippet: Currently, there are no cures for prion diseases, which are a group of fatal neurodegenerative disorders. However, researchers are actively working on developing potential treatments, including therapies that target the abnormal prion protein or interfere with its conversion process. These approaches include immunotherapy, gene therapy, and small-molecule drugs.
snippet_highlighted_words: immunotherapy, gene therapy, and small-molecule drugs

list.title: Immunotherapy:
list.snippet: This approach involves using antibodies or other immune system components to target and neutralize the abnormal prion protein (PrPSc) or to stimulate the body's own immune response against it.

list.title: Gene Therapy:
list.snippet: Gene therapy aims to reduce the production of the normal prion protein (PrPC), which is necessary for the replication of the abnormal prion protein, or to correct the genetic defect that causes certain inherited forms of prion disease.

list.title: Small-Molecule Drugs:
list.snippet: Scientists are investigating various small molecules that can inhibit the conversion of normal prion protein to the abnormal form or help clear existing abnormal prion protein from the brain.

list.title: Epigenetic Editing:
list.snippet: This approach involves using molecular tools to turn off the gene that produces the prion protein, effectively preventing its production without altering the underlying DNA sequence.

list.title: Base Editing:
list.snippet: Base editing is a type of gene editing that can make precise changes to the DNA sequence. Researchers have used base editing to reduce levels of the disease-causing prion protein in a mouse model of prion disease, which significantly extended their lifespan.

text_blocks.snippet: Early diagnosis of prion disease is crucial for potential treatment, as some therapies may be more effective when administered before significant brain damage has occurred.
Researchers are actively exploring various therapeutic strategies, including:

list.snippet: Developing new and improved versions of existing therapies, such as antibodies and gene therapies.
Identifying new drug targets and developing new drugs that can effectively inhibit prion protein conversion or clear abnormal prion protein.
Conducting clinical trials to evaluate the safety and efficacy of potential treatments in humans.
Developing new diagnostic tools to detect prion disease earlier and more accurately.
Prion diseases are rare and complex, making it challenging to conduct large-scale clinical trials.
The blood-brain barrier can make it difficult to deliver drugs to the brain.
The prion protein is essential for normal brain function, so any treatment that reduces its levels must be carefully designed to minimize side effects.
